Spring Bulbs.fact: Most spring bulbs are planted in autumn so they can rest through the cold of winter.

Summer Flowers.fact: Removing faded blooms often encourages annual flowers to keep blooming for longer.

Roses.fact: Roses are usually pruned in late winter or early spring, just as new growth begins.

Herb Garden.fact: Mint spreads quickly, so many gardeners grow it in a pot to keep it in check.

Vegetable Patch.fact: Radishes grow fast and are often ready to pick in about four weeks.

Tomato Time.fact: Tomatoes ripen best with plenty of warm sunshine, ideally six hours or more a day.

Berry Patch.fact: Blueberries like acidic soil, so many gardeners grow them in containers of special mix.

Orchard Fruit.fact: Many fruit trees crop better when another variety grows nearby to help pollination.

Citrus Grove.fact: In cooler climates, citrus trees are often grown in pots and brought indoors for winter.

Houseplants.fact: Overwatering harms more houseplants than forgetting to water, so check the soil first.

Succulents.fact: Succulents store water in thick leaves, so they like a deep soak followed by a dry spell.

Garden Tools.fact: Clean and dry your tools before storing them to keep them sharp and rust free.

Rich Soil.fact: A single handful of healthy soil can hold billions of tiny living organisms.

Compost Heap.fact: A good heap balances greens like fresh clippings with browns like dry leaves.

Watering Wisely.fact: Watering deeply but less often encourages plants to grow stronger, deeper roots.

Pollinators.fact: Planting flowers in clusters makes it easier for bees to find them.

Honey Bees.fact: A honeybee makes only a tiny fraction of a teaspoon of honey in its whole life.

Butterfly Garden.fact: Monarch caterpillars feed only on milkweed, so planting it helps this butterfly.

Backyard Birds.fact: A shallow birdbath with fresh water attracts birds as well as food does.

Birdhouse Time.fact: Birdhouses are best put up in late winter, ready for the spring nesting season.

Wildflowers.fact: Wildflower meadows do best in poor soil, where grasses cannot crowd out the flowers.

Cottage Garden.fact: Cottage gardens mix flowers, herbs and vegetables together in relaxed, colorful borders.

Lavender Fields.fact: Lavender thrives in sunny spots with well-drained soil and little water once settled.

Sunflowers.fact: Young sunflower heads turn to follow the sun across the sky each day.

Ferns and Moss.fact: Ferns reproduce by tiny spores instead of seeds.

Shade Garden.fact: Many shade plants have large leaves to catch as much light as possible.

Trees.fact: A tree trunk usually adds one ring for each year of growth.

Flowering Trees.fact: Plant flowering trees where you can enjoy them from a window in spring.

Shrubs.fact: Hydrangea flower color can change with the acidity of the soil.

Hedges and Borders.fact: Trim hedges so the base is slightly wider than the top, letting light reach lower leaves.

Lawn Care.fact: Mowing a little higher helps grass grow deeper roots and cope with dry spells.

Common Weeds.fact: Mulching around plants blocks light so fewer weed seeds can sprout.

Mulch Matters.fact: A layer of mulch two to three inches deep helps soil hold moisture.

Seeds and Sowing.fact: Check the seed packet for sowing depth; a common guide is about twice the seed's width.

Planting Day.fact: Plant on a cloudy day or in the evening so young plants can settle before the heat.

Autumn Garden.fact: Autumn is a great time to plant trees and shrubs because the soil is still warm.

Winter Garden.fact: Dormant plants are resting, not dead, and many need winter chill to flower later.

Greenhouse.fact: A greenhouse can stretch the growing season by weeks at both ends of the year.

Container Gardening.fact: Every pot needs drainage holes so roots never sit in soggy soil.

Hanging Baskets.fact: Hanging baskets dry out quickly, so they often need water every day in summer.

Raised Beds.fact: Raised beds are easier on the back and warm up faster in spring.

Climbing Plants.fact: Twining plants wrap around supports, while others cling with tendrils or sticky pads.

Pumpkin Patch.fact: Pumpkins need lots of space, and their vines can spread many feet across the garden.

Potato Patch.fact: Potato plants are earthed up with soil to protect the tubers from light.

Salad Bowl.fact: Cut-and-come-again lettuce regrows after harvesting, giving several pickings.

Peppers and Chiles.fact: Most of a pepper's heat comes from the white ribs inside rather than the seeds.

Root Vegetables.fact: Loose, stone-free soil helps root vegetables grow long and straight.

Onion Family.fact: Garlic is usually planted in autumn from individual cloves.

Squash Family.fact: Zucchini flowers are edible and can be stuffed or fried.

Cabbage Family.fact: Cover brassicas with fine netting to keep butterflies from laying eggs on the leaves.

Corn and Grains.fact: Corn is wind-pollinated, so plant it in blocks rather than a single long row.

Beans.fact: Beans can add nitrogen to the soil through helpful bacteria on their roots.

Peas.fact: Peas prefer cool weather, so sow them early in spring.

Melon Patch.fact: A ripe watermelon often has a yellowish patch where it rested on the ground.

Grapes and Vines.fact: Grapevines fruit on new shoots, which is why they are pruned hard in winter.

Nut Trees.fact: Many nut trees take several years to begin producing, so planting early pays off.

Garden Pests.fact: Ladybugs and lacewings eat aphids, so welcoming them helps protect your plants.

Helpful Insects.fact: Many insects in the garden are helpers that eat pests or pollinate plants.

Garden Wildlife.fact: A toad in the garden can eat many insects and slugs in a single night.

Pond Life.fact: Even a small pond can become a haven for frogs, dragonflies and birds.

Water Features.fact: The gentle sound of running water can make a garden feel calmer.

Garden Paths.fact: Curved paths invite you to wander and reveal the garden a little at a time.

Garden Seating.fact: A shady seat near your favorite flowers is the best spot for a coffee break.

Garden Decor.fact: A sundial tells the time by the shadow the sun casts.

From Garden to Table.fact: Fresh herbs add the most flavor when stirred in just before serving.

Jam and Preserves.fact: Fruit jams set because of natural pectin, found in apples and citrus peel.

Tea Garden.fact: Many herbal teas can be brewed from leaves and flowers you grow yourself.

Cut Flowers.fact: Cut flowers in the cool of the morning and put the stems straight into water.

Dried Flowers.fact: Hang flower bunches upside down in a dry, dark place to keep their color.

Flower Arranging.fact: An odd number of stems often looks more natural in an arrangement.

Orchids.fact: Many orchids grow on trees in the wild and take moisture from the air.

African Violets.fact: African violets dislike cold water on their fuzzy leaves, so many people water from below.

Cacti.fact: A cactus spine is really a modified leaf.

Bonsai.fact: Bonsai is the art of growing tiny trees in shallow containers, shaped over many years.

Japanese Garden.fact: Raked gravel in a Japanese garden often stands for flowing water.

English Garden.fact: Topiary is the art of clipping shrubs into shapes such as spheres, cones and animals.

Tropical Garden.fact: Many tropical plants must come indoors when temperatures drop in autumn.

Desert Garden.fact: Xeriscaping uses drought-tolerant plants to save water in dry climates.

Rock Garden.fact: Alpine plants like gritty, fast-draining soil that copies mountain slopes.

Meadow.fact: Meadows are usually mown once a year, after wildflowers have set seed.

Saving Seeds.fact: Seeds saved from heirloom plants will grow true to type.

Propagation.fact: Many houseplants root easily from a cutting placed in a glass of water.

Pruning Basics.fact: Make pruning cuts just above a bud, sloping slightly away from it.

Garden Safety.fact: Take short breaks to drink water and stretch, especially on warm days.

Sun and Shade.fact: Most vegetables need at least six hours of direct sunlight a day.

Garden Weather.fact: A rain gauge shows how much water your garden has really received.

Plant Food.fact: Plants use three main nutrients: nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

Garden Journal.fact: A simple garden journal helps you remember what grew well and when to plant next year.

Garden Planning.fact: Rotating vegetable crops each year helps keep soil healthy.

Feeding the Birds.fact: Cleaning feeders regularly helps keep visiting birds healthy.

Farmers Market.fact: Produce often tastes best when picked ripe and eaten within a day or two.

Community Garden.fact: Community gardens bring neighbors together and put unused land to good use.

Garden History.fact: Maze and knot gardens became fashionable in European gardens hundreds of years ago.

Flower Emblems.fact: Many countries and regions choose a national or state flower as a symbol.

Edible Flowers.fact: Only eat flowers you are sure are safe and that were grown without chemical sprays.

Pressed Flowers.fact: Flowers pressed between sheets of paper inside a heavy book dry flat in a few weeks.

Garden Sounds.fact: Gardens full of flowers, trees and water often have a wonderful variety of sounds.

Backyard Barbecue.fact: Fresh rosemary from the garden adds a lovely smoky flavor on the grill.

Kids in the Garden.fact: Fast growers like sunflowers and radishes are great for gardening with children.

The Gardener's Reward.fact: Many people find that time in a garden helps them feel calm and relaxed.
